answers.question: List of scenarios
answers.answer:
MCK uses three climate scenarios:
1. 1.5°C Orderly Scenario – Net zero 2050: A world where global warming is successfully limited to 1.5 degrees above pre-industrial levels, as ambitious goals and policies to reduce greenhouse gas emissions are immediately and effectively implemented.
2. 2.0°C Disorderly Scenario – Delayed transition: A world where global warming is limited to 2.0 degrees above pre-industrial levels, as policies to reduce greenhouse gas emissions are introduced after 2030. There is a rapid and concerted effort to reach net zero 2050 goals.
3. 3.0°C Hot House World Scenario – Current trajectory: A world where global warming reaches 3.0 degrees above pre-industrial levels by 2100, due to no additional policies introduced to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
answers.evidence: "3.0°C Hot House World Scenario – Current trajectory: A world where global warming reaches 3.0 degrees above preindustrial levels by 2100, due to no additional policies introduced to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. 2.0°C Disorderly Scenario – Delayed transition: A world where global warming is limited to 2.0 degrees above preindustrial levels, as policies to reduce greenhouse gas emissions are introduced after 2030. There is a rapid and concerted effort to reach net zero 2050 goals. 1.5°C Orderly Scenario – Net zero 2050: A world where global warming is successfully limited to 1.5 degrees above preindustrial levels, as ambitious goals and policies to reduce greenhouse gas emissions are immediately and effectively implemented."
answers.location_hint: Page 10, Strategy section; also Appendix A, pages 26-27
answers.notes: These three scenarios align with the mandated NZ CS scenarios: (i) at least one 1.5°C Paris Agreement-aligned scenario, (ii) a greater than 3°C-aligned high warming scenario, and (iii) a third scenario (the 2.0°C Disorderly).

answers.answer:
The document describes three scenarios with the following global temperature outcomes by 2100:
1. 1.5°C Orderly Scenario – global warming successfully limited to 1.5 degrees above pre-industrial levels
2. 2.0°C Disorderly Scenario – global warming limited to 2.0 degrees above pre-industrial levels
3. 3.0°C Hot House World Scenario – global warming reaches 3.0 degrees above pre-industrial levels

answers.question: Scenario provider
answers.answer: The Aotearoa Circle (tourism sector scenarios) and Beca Limited for Te Kaunihera Hanganga Tautaiao | New Zealand Green Building Council (NZGBC) (property sector scenarios). WSP New Zealand Ltd was engaged to undertake a peer review of the scenarios.
answers.evidence: "MCK considered the work undertaken by the Aotearoa Circle to develop climate scenarios for the tourism sector as a whole. Given that MCK is an owner operator of hotels and has significant physical assets, we have also had regard to the sector scenarios developed by Beca Limited for Te Kaunihera Hanganga Tautaiao | New Zealand Green Building Council (NZGBC)." and "MCK engaged WSP to undertake a peer review of the scenarios and provide recommendations for further development."
answers.notes: MCK drew on sector scenarios from two providers (Aotearoa Circle for tourism, Beca Limited for property/construction via NZGBC), and had WSP peer review the scenarios. The entity-level scenarios were developed internally using these as a basis.

answers.question: Pick-and-mix of SSPs and RCPs
answers.answer: MCK uses SSP3-7.0 for physical climate risk exposure assessment (aligned to the Hot House scenario). The three transition/physical scenarios are framed in terms of temperature outcomes (1.5°C Orderly, 2.0°C Disorderly, 3.0°C Hot House) without explicit RCP labels. Only SSP3-7.0 is explicitly named in the document.
answers.evidence: "SSP3-7.0 climate change projection scenario was used for this exposure assessment. This aligns to the Hot house scenario and of the five IPCC scenarios, it is one of the upper middle warming scenarios for which NIWA data is available."
answers.notes: The document explicitly names SSP3-7.0 for the physical exposure assessment. The three narrative scenarios (1.5°C Orderly, 2.0°C Disorderly, 3.0°C Hot House) are described without explicit SSP or RCP labels beyond SSP3-7.0 for the Hot House physical assessment. No RCP labels are used anywhere in the document.

answers.question: Customised scenarios
answers.notes: The document references use of the Tourism Sector Climate Scenarios and the Construction and Property Sector Climate Scenarios (Orderly, Disorderly, and Hot House), but there is no mention of customised/bespoke scenarios developed by MCK itself. The scenarios used appear to be standard sector-level scenarios, not customised ones.

answers.question: Co-produced climate scenarios
answers.answer: MCK's climate scenarios were not fully co-produced with external parties, but were developed using internal staff resources and working groups, with support and peer review by external experts (WSP), and workshops with senior leadership, Hotel General Managers and Directors. MCK drew on sector scenarios developed by the Aotearoa Circle (tourism sector) and Beca Limited for the New Zealand Green Building Council (NZGBC) (property and construction sector), tailoring these into entity-level scenarios for its own business.
answers.evidence: "MCK undertook scenario analysis using internal staff resources and working groups led by the Vice President Legal and Sustainabilty Manager; support and peer review by external experts; and workshops with senior leadership, Hotel General Managers and Directors... MCK considered the work undertaken by the Aotearoa Circle to develop climate scenarios and adaptation strategies for the tourism sector as a whole... we have also had regard to the sector scenarios developed by Beca Limited for Te Kaunihera Hanganga Tautaiao | New Zealand Green Building Council (NZGBC)."
answers.notes: Scenarios were internally developed with external peer review (WSP) and drew on pre-existing sector scenarios from the Aotearoa Circle and NZGBC/Beca. They were not co-produced in a formal collaborative sense with external stakeholders, but were informed by external sector work and reviewed by external experts.

3. **3.0°C Hot House World Scenario – Current trajectory**: A world where global warming reaches 3.0 degrees above pre-industrial levels by 2100, due to no additional policies introduced to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

answers.question: Model used
answers.notes: The context does not specify a particular climate model (e.g., a specific GCM or IAM such as REMIND, MESSAGE, or GCAM) used in the scenario analysis. MCK references sector scenarios from the Aotearoa Circle and Beca Limited/NZGBC, but no specific underlying climate model is named.

answers.question: Damage from acute physical risk considered
answers.answer: Yes. MCK considered damage from acute physical risks including flooding, coastal inundation, coastal erosion, landslides, and sea level rise. In FY24, no hotels suffered significant damage. Some remedial actions have been taken (e.g., protection of electrical services, on-site sandbags, basement pumps to reduce flood impact). Overall portfolio physical risk is rated Low across all geohazard categories, with the exception of coastal inundation rated as moderate for 2 hotels.
answers.evidence: "Currently, impacts from acute physical climate-related events on our hotels and business operations are rare. Occasionally, bookings or access to some hotels can be affected by weather events for short periods of time, however these events are not often attributable to climate change and do not generally disrupt operations... There were no cases where MCK hotels suffered any significant damage or disruption to guests in 2024... We have already taken some remedial action to reduce the vulnerability of our hotels at greatest risk to acute physical climate impacts (such as protection of electrical services; on site sandbags; and basement pumps to reduce flood impact)."
answers.notes: The document explicitly addresses acute physical risks (flooding, coastal inundation, erosion, landslides, sea level rise) and confirms no material damage occurred in FY24, while noting some mitigation measures already in place.

answers.question: Non-temperature variables in scenarios
answers.answer:
The scenarios include the following non-temperature variables as Key 2050 Indicators: Sea level rise, NZ native forestry (hectares), Number of hot days >25°C, Extreme rainfall, Whole of life building emission reduction requirement, Carbon price (NZD/tonne), and NZ net emissions (MtCO2e). Specific values across the three scenarios are:

- **Orderly (1.5°C):** Sea level rise 0.2m, NZ native forestry 0.8mha, +15 hot days, +15% extreme rainfall, 90% building emission reduction, $277 NZD/tonne carbon price, 6 MtCO2e net emissions
- **Disorderly (2.0°C):** Sea level rise 0.22m, NZ native forestry 0.5mha, +20 hot days, +18% extreme rainfall, 80% building emission reduction, $369 NZD/tonne carbon price, 24 MtCO2e net emissions
- **Hot House (3.0°C):** Sea level rise 0.32m, NZ native forestry 0.2mha, +30 hot days, +22% extreme rainfall, 50% building emission reduction, $35 NZD/tonne carbon price, 40 MtCO2e net emissions
answers.evidence: "Key 2050 Indicators: Sea level rise | NZ native forestry | Number of hot days >25C | Extreme rainfall | Whole of life building emission reduction requirement | Carbon price | NZ net emissions" with values for Orderly: "0.2m | 0.8mha | +15 days | +15% | 90% | $277 $NZD/tonne | 6MtCO2e"; Disorderly: "0.22m | 0.5mha | +20 days | +18% | 80% | $369 $NZD/tonne | 24MtCO2e"; Hot House: "0.32m | 0.2mha | +30 days | +22% | 50% | $35 $NZD/tonne | 40MtCO2e"
answers.notes: Sea level rise figures are relative to 2005; number of hot days and rainfall figures are 2040 relative to 1990, as noted in footnotes 5/8/11. Building emission reduction requirement is drawn from the Construction and Property Sector Climate Scenarios.

answers.question: Scale of scenarios
answers.answer: MCK's entity-level scenarios are downscaled from sector-level scenarios. The scenarios draw from and are consistent with the Tourism Sector Climate Scenarios and the Construction and Property Sector Climate Scenarios, but are "downscaled for our business." They operate at the entity level, covering MCK's owned and managed hotels and landholdings in New Zealand, with a global narrative context underpinning each scenario.
answers.evidence: "MCK's entity-level scenarios draw from, and are consistent with, the sector scenarios (but downscaled for our business) and therefore support comparability with the disclosures of others in our sector."
answers.notes: The scenarios are applied at the entity level (MCK's hotel portfolio in New Zealand), downscaled from sector-level scenarios developed for the tourism sector and the construction and property sector. Global narratives are included as context for each scenario (1.5°C Orderly, 2.0°C Disorderly, 3.0°C Hot House).

answers.question: Time frames
answers.answer:
MCK uses three time horizons for climate-related risks and opportunities:
- Short-term: Present–2030 (impacts on near-term income, operating costs and increased repairs and maintenance)
- Medium-term: 2031–2045 (7–10 year refurbishment cycle; impacts on core aspects of strategy, acquisition of new hotels, expansion of the portfolio, development phasing and/or divestment decisions)
- Long-term: 2046–2075 (30–50 year life of primary property assets; impacts from travel patterns, trading conditions and long-term viability)

For physical climate variables, time frames are aligned to MfE guidance: short-term (2021–2040), medium-term (2041–2060), and long-term (2081–2100).

Noting that our assessment of physical climate variables across our portfolio has been aligned to time frames consistent with MfE guidance, i.e. short-term (2021–2040), medium-term (2041–2060) and long-term (2081–2100).

answers.question: Justification for scenario/model choice
answers.answer: MCK justified its scenario choices on several grounds: (1) The Orderly and Hot House world scenarios align with the mandated NZ CS scenarios (i.e., at least one 1.5°C Paris Agreement-aligned scenario, a >3°C high warming scenario, and a third scenario). (2) The Disorderly scenario was selected to represent a challenging future as it is designed to explore a disrupted climate transition. (3) Scenarios were drawn from and are consistent with sector scenarios developed by the Aotearoa Circle (tourism sector) and Beca Limited for NZGBC (property/construction sector), supporting comparability with others in the same sectors. (4) The sector scenarios are based on a coherent set of socio-economic assumptions, decarbonisation pathways, and climate change projections. (5) Entity-level scenarios were downscaled from sector scenarios to reflect MCK's specific circumstances as an amalgam of both tourism and property sectors.
answers.evidence: "Our Orderly and Hot House world scenarios, align with the mandated NZ CS scenarios. We selected our remaining Disorderly scenario, to represent a challenging future for our business as it is designed to explore a disrupted climate transition. No additional scenarios have been explored." and "MCK considered the work undertaken by the Aotearoa Circle to develop climate scenarios and adaptation strategies for the tourism sector as a whole. Given that MCK is an owner operator of hotels and has significant physical assets, we have also had regard to the sector scenarios developed by Beca Limited for Te Kaunihera Hanganga Tautaiao | New Zealand Green Building Council (NZGBC). These sector Orderly, Disorderly and Hot house world scenarios are based on a coherent set of socio-economic assumptions, decarbonisation pathways, and climate change projections." and "MCK's entity-level scenarios draw from, and are consistent with, the sector scenarios (but downscaled for our business) and therefore support comparability with the disclosures of others in our sector."
answers.notes: The mandated NZ CS scenario requirements are also footnoted: (i) at least one 1.5°C Paris Agreement-aligned scenario, (ii) a >3°C high warming scenario, and (iii) a third scenario.

answers.question: Historic climate impacts
answers.answer: MCK considers climate-related physical and transition impacts to be overall immaterial for 2024. Impacts from acute physical climate-related events on hotels and business operations are rare. In 2024, few climate-related acute weather events attributable to climate change occurred in NZ. No hotels were located in areas that flooded or experienced landslips, coastal erosion or inundation. There were no cases where MCK hotels suffered any significant damage or disruption to guests, nor any material supply chain disruptions. There were no material low-emission upgrades or resilience measures undertaken in response to climate-related weather events or regulations. Access to capital was not impacted, nor were any acquisition or divestment decisions affected. No climate-related opportunities were identified or pursued in 2024. As a result, there are no climate-related material financial impacts reported for the 2024 financial year.
answers.evidence: "We consider climate-related physical and transition impacts to be overall immaterial for MCK for 2024... Currently, impacts from acute physical climate-related events on our hotels and business operations are rare. Occasionally, bookings or access to some hotels can be affected by weather events for short periods of time, however these events are not often attributable to climate change and do not generally disrupt operations. Few climate-related acute weather events attributable to climate change occurred in NZ during 2024. Our portfolio showed resilience during 2024 events that resulted in flooding, no hotels were located in areas that flooded or experienced landslips, coastal erosion or inundation this year. There were no cases where MCK hotels suffered any significant damage or disruption to guests in 2024, nor were there any material supply chain disruptions impacting our business from climate-related physical or transition impacts. There were no material (low emission) upgrades or resilience measures undertaken across the portfolio in 2024 in response to climate-related weather events or regulations. Access to capital has not been impacted, nor were any acquisition or divestment decisions affected in 2024... Given there are no material current climate impacts identified in 2024, there are no climate-related material financial impacts reported for the 2024 financial year."
answers.notes: The document clearly states that all climate-related physical and transition impacts were immaterial for FY24, with no significant damage, disruption, or financial impacts recorded.

answers.question: Direct and indirect physical climate risks
answers.answer: MCK identifies both acute and chronic physical climate risks. Acute risks include climate-related geohazards such as: Sea Level Rise, Coastal Inundation, Coastal Erosion, Rainfall-induced landslides, and Flooding. Chronic risks relate to climate change variables (e.g., temperature changes). In 2024, MCK engaged WSP to assess the physical exposure of its hotel portfolio. The assessment found that the majority of the portfolio (35%) has no or low vulnerability to climate-related geohazards and climate variables, while 3 hotels (18%) are at high risk from one geohazard (either some impact from flooding, or coastal inundation accounting for future sea level rise). During 2024, no hotels were located in areas that flooded or experienced landslips, coastal erosion or inundation, and there were no cases of significant damage or disruption to guests.
answers.evidence: "and land assets, the majority of our portfolio has no or low vulnerability to climate-related geohazards and climate variables (35%). Overall, just 3 hotels (18%) are at high risk from one geohazard (either some impact from flooding, or coastal inundation accounting for future sea level rise)." / "Our portfolio showed resilience during 2024 events that resulted in flooding, no hotels were located in areas that flooded or experienced landslips, coastal erosion or inundation this year. There were no cases where MCK hotels suffered any significant damage or disruption to guests in 2024." / "Climate-related geohazard: Hazards specifically related to geological or environmental processes that may be influenced by climate change factors such as changes to rainfall, these include: Sea Level Rise... Coastal Inundation... Coastal Erosion... Rainfall induced landslides... Flooding..."
answers.notes: Physical risks are categorised as acute (geohazards) and chronic (climate change variables). The document also notes that coastal MCK properties face particular risk of insurance retreat due to physical risks. Supply chain physical climate risks are not yet included in the risk assessment.
